title: Adversarial convex bandits with exact one-point value feedback
summary: The environment precommits to a sequence of bounded convex losses. Each round, the learner acts in the unit ball and observes only the exact loss at its action. There is no observation noise; difficulty comes from the changing functions and one-point feedback.

description_paragraphs: The environment precommits to a sequence of bounded convex losses. Each round, the learner acts in the unit ball and observes only the exact loss at its action. There is no observation noise; difficulty comes from the changing functions and one-point feedback.

model.instance: Before interaction, the environment fixes convex losses $f_t:B_2^d(1)\to[0,1]$. No smoothness, Lipschitz continuity, or continuity is promised. Each round reveals only the exact action-point value.

assumptions.description: Every f_t is convex on the unit ball. Differentiability, continuity, and Lipschitz regularity are not additionally assumed.

interaction_timing: The environment precommits to every f_t.
The next round permits queries only at selected points of the new function f_{t+1}.
model.adversary_information: The environment fixes the entire loss sequence before interaction. It may know the algorithm and public parameters but cannot depend on the learner’s private seed. This is an oblivious-adversary specification and does not automatically extend to history-dependent adaptive adversaries.
unresolved_applicability: The strongest current upper bound and the computable upper bound optimize different costs. Smoothness of the domain boundary cannot be added as an unstated assumption.
description_paragraphs: The unknown current convex function $f_t$ takes values in $[0,1]$ at all feasible points. No Lipschitz bound or continuity at the boundary of the closed domain is assumed. Define the comparator using the infimum and do not add an attainment assumption.
The action and sole value-query point is $x_t$. The same point incurs and returns the loss.
Require $d,T\ge1$; actual actions and query points lie in the Euclidean unit ball.

operations.query_signature: Input: $t,\ x_t\in B_2^d(1)$. The specification's protocol governs timing and visible information.
operations.order_convention: order is relative to the current member f_t(x), f(x), or sample F(x;ξ_t) of the named indexed function family and only with respect to x; finite feedback interfaces have no derivative order

feedback_quality.description: Choose x_t, then receive one exact value. No gradient, second point, additional noise, or full-function feedback is provided. Successive functions may be entirely different, so cross-round value differences are not finite differences of one function.

operations.coupling: Choose x_t, then receive one exact value. No gradient, second point, additional noise, or full-function feedback is provided. Successive functions may be entirely different, so cross-round value differences are not finite differences of one function.
operations.index_control: The learner selects feasible actions and explicitly permitted probes. The environment controls the current loss, outcome, or fresh sample; the learner cannot select future rounds.
operations.access_schedule: Follow the interaction order in registry.protocols exactly. Current loss feedback follows the action; any pre-action context or advice phase is specified separately.

public_inputs: Function values in $[0,1]$ and a convexity assumption
auxiliary_interfaces: No additional access to hidden losses, means, or gradients is available. Projection, sampling, and internal optimization over public domains may have separately recorded computation costs; they are not free loss oracles.
description_paragraphs: Exact function value at the action point:
Choose $x_t$ first, then receive one exact function value at that point.
No gradient, second point, extra noise, or full-function feedback is supplied.
Consecutive-round functions may differ completely. A difference of values across rounds is not a finite difference of one function.
Public inputs are $d,T$, the unit-ball domain, the value range $[0,1]$, and convexity.

output.feasibility: Every loss-bearing action must belong to the action domain. The final output retains the complete action trajectory.
output.allowed_postprocessing: Any measurable computation on received feedback is allowed. No native observation may be added after the budget is exhausted or the algorithm stops.
output.certificate_requirement: Only the stated statistical guarantee is required, not a certificate verifiable through the feedback interface.
description_paragraphs: The output is the complete action trajectory satisfying feasibility and timing requirements. Randomized mixtures may be implemented before acting. Retrospective averages or convex combinations cannot replace actions that have already incurred loss. No additional optimal value or certificate is required.

metric.normalization: Use the cumulative quantity over T rounds without dividing by T. Preserve the displayed order of probability or expectation.
metric.finiteness_conditions: Both cumulative losses lie in [0,T], so their difference on each execution path lies in [-T,T].

algorithms.randomization: Private randomization is allowed. The seed is hidden from the environment and independent of the fixed instance and sample randomness.
algorithms.adaptivity: The action and every probe in a round may depend only on previous-round feedback, public inputs, any context or advice already revealed that round, and private randomness. They may not use unrevealed current losses or samples.
restrictions: All measurable causal policies satisfying the declared information timing and feasible domain are allowed, without extra span, iteration-form, or polynomial-time restrictions.
algorithms.internal_computation: Arbitrary measurable causal policies and exact internal arithmetic are allowed. Feedback complexity alone does not determine arithmetic or bit complexity. The 2020 upper bound is an information-theoretic existence result; its feedback count does not establish an implementable polynomial-time algorithm.
algorithms.parallelism: Online rounds proceed sequentially. A two-point evaluation is a same-round feedback pair, not two independent rounds.
description_paragraphs: All measurable causal randomized policies respecting the stated timing are allowed. The private seed is independent of the fixed instance and future samples. Apart from explicit feedback, output, and budget requirements, there are no restrictions on linear spans, iteration form, internal arithmetic, memory, or communication.

guarantees.complete_expression: The native objective is $\inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_{f_{1:T}}\mathbb E_{\mathcal A}[R_T]$.
aggregation_order: First take the infimum over complete nonanticipating learning policies using only public inputs.
Then take the supremum over instances fixed before interaction and satisfying the model assumptions.
Expectation includes learner randomness and any sampling or observation noise.
Fixed, per-round, and sample-path comparators are distinguished exactly as in the target expression.
guarantees.quantifier_order: One learning algorithm must apply to every instance in the declared class. It may use public inputs only, not hidden instance parameters.
guarantees.time_uniformity: The T-round horizon is fixed and public. No anytime or simultaneous-all-T high-probability guarantee is implied.
description_paragraphs: Choose one algorithm using public inputs before taking the worst case over all admissible instances. Expectation covers the algorithm's private randomness and the observation randomness specified by the model. Comparator choice and the order of summation, minimization, and expectation follow the displayed formula.

quantities.expression: R*_T = inf_{A in admissible nonanticipating randomized learners} sup_{I in declared model} E_A,I[sum_t f_t(x_t)−inf_u sum_t f_t(u)].
quantities.analysis_scope: Compare only this specification and the listed parameter regions.
quantities.comparison_note: The comparator is an infimum; bounded convex losses on a closed domain need not attain their infimum without a boundary continuity/lower-semicontinuity promise.
quantities.expression_latex: \begin{aligned}\mathcal R_T^*&=\inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_{f_{1:T}\in\mathcal I}\mathbb E_{\mathcal A}[R_T],\\ R_T&=\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-\inf_{u\in B_2^d(1)}\sum_{t=1}^T f_t(u).\end{aligned}

bounds.derivation: Use $f_t(x)=(1+\varepsilon_t x_1)/2$ with independent uniform signs $\varepsilon_t$. The functions are convex and take values in $[0,1]$. The learner's centered loss has zero expectation, while the hindsight action gains $\mathbb E|\sum_t\varepsilon_t|/2$. The lower bound holds even with full-gradient feedback, so it also applies to one-value feedback.

evidence.supports: Supports the stated results and explicit reductions: $\mathcal{R}_T^*\le C d^{5/2}\sqrt T\log(2T)$; $\mathcal{R}_T^*\le T$. Each bound retains its own model, feedback, parameter region, and quantifiers.
notes: For adversarial convex losses on the unit ball, exact one-point feedback, and value range $[0,1]$, the source gives $Cd^{5/2}\sqrt T\log(2T)$. This is an information-theoretic upper bound without an efficient-internal-computation guarantee.

evidence.supports: Supports the stated results and explicit reductions: $\mathcal{R}_T^*\ge c\sqrt T$. Each bound retains its own model, feedback, parameter region, and quantifiers.
notes: The source lower bound is $\Omega(L\sqrt{T(D^2+DP)})$, with path budget in $[0,TD]$. An independent one-dimensional block construction on the Euclidean ball also checks the correspondence between geometry and path length.
